cli.group.checks: Checks for a pipeline and for this computer
cli.group.sources: Settings from a file or a profile
cli.switch: No value: the option alone turns it on
column.avg: The average packet size on this connection, in bytes.
column.down: Data that actually reached the program on this connection. The unit beside the number changes with its size.
column.down_seen: Data the tool captured coming in, before any impairment. The difference from the delivered download is what never arrived.
column.dropped: Packets of this connection dropped by the impairments: loss, link outages, cut networks, resets and the rest.
column.dur: Seconds between the first and the last packet of the connection in this session.
column.ice: For a call or another connection that uses ICE, such as WebRTC: which path it takes, read from its STUN messages. LAN, NAT, WAN, TURN or STUN.
column.idle: Seconds since the connection's last packet. It stops counting when the session stops.
column.kb: Everything that got through on this connection, both directions together.
column.local_port: The port on this computer, which is what links the connection to a program. Empty for traffic with no ports.
column.packets: Packets seen on this connection since it appeared.
column.pid: The process id that owns the local port.
column.proc: The program that opened the connection, read when the connection first appeared, so a row can still name a program that has closed since. A question mark means the name could not be read; starting the program as administrator usually helps.
column.proto: The transport protocol: TCP, UDP, ICMP or IP.
column.remote_ip: The address this computer is talking to. Right-click a row to aim the impairments at it.
column.remote_port: The port on the far side, such as 443 for HTTPS or 53 for DNS. Empty for traffic with no ports, such as ping.
column.scoped: How much of the connection was in impairment scope: yes for all of its packets, no for none, or a share such as 97 percent when the targeting left some out.
column.up: Data that actually left this computer on this connection.
column.up_seen: Data the tool captured going out, before any impairment. The difference from the delivered upload is what never left.
counter.corrupted: Packets that arrived with one bit of their data flipped. A packet with no data, such as a bare acknowledgement, cannot be damaged and passes, so this can stay below the share you set.
counter.down: How fast data is coming in right now, in kilobytes per second.
counter.driver_dropped: Linux only: packets the capture driver dropped before the tool saw them, because its queue was full. The tool lost them, not a setting of yours. Narrow the traffic filter so less goes through the tool.
counter.drop_block: Packets dropped by a blocking rule.
counter.drop_flap: Packets dropped by a link outage. Counted apart from loss.
counter.drop_internet_only: Packets to or from the local network, dropped by the switch that cuts it.
counter.drop_lan: Packets to or from the internet, dropped by the switch that cuts the internet.
counter.drop_loss: Packets dropped by the loss you set. Link outages are counted on their own.
counter.drop_mtu: Packets dropped as too large by the size limit (the MTU black hole).
counter.drop_nat: Packets dropped because their connection's NAT mapping had expired.
counter.drop_overflow: Packets dropped because the tool's queue overflowed under heavy load. These are packets the tool lost, not the link you set, so they always count all captured traffic and are not part of the effective loss.
counter.drop_rate: Packets dropped because the speed limit's queue was full: more data kept coming than the limit and its buffer could hold. Counted apart from loss.
counter.drop_rst: Packets of connections the tool reset.
counter.drop_send: Packets the tool captured but could not put back on the wire, for example because the connection went down. The tool lost them, not the network, so they are not part of the effective loss.
counter.drop_shutdown: Packets still waiting in the tool when you pressed {{app.buttons.stop}}. The network did not lose them: the session ended before they were released.
counter.drop_syn: Connection-opening packets dropped by the SYN setting.
counter.flap_held: How many packets link outages have held back instead of dropping, since the session started. It only grows; what is waiting right now is in the queue.
counter.kernel_bypassed: Linux only: packets that went around the tool without being impaired, because the kernel's buffer in front of it was full. They are not in the packet count. Narrow the traffic filter so less goes through the tool.
counter.loss_bursts: How many runs of lost packets the session produced, when losses come in a row. Zero with runs set means the session was too short to see one, or the loss is 100 percent, so there are no separate runs to count.
counter.queue: How many packets are waiting in the tool right now. It grows with latency or a speed limit and falls back when they are released.
counter.reordered: Packets that left the tool in a different order than they came in. Zero with jitter or spikes set means the packets were too far apart for one to overtake another.
counter.rst_sent: How many reset packets the tool sent to tear connections down.
counter.seen: How many packets have passed through the tool since the session started.
counter.up: How fast data is going out right now, in kilobytes per second.
csv.conn.captured_total_bytes: The two captured columns added together: everything the connection offered, before any impairment.
csv.conn.packets_in_scope: How many of the connection's packets were in impairment scope: the number behind the share in {{app.conns.scoped}}.
csv.ports: Every row of a port check: the ports, the protocol and IP version, whether they are free, and who holds or listens on them.
csv.scan: Every row of a port scan: the address and ports, the protocol, the state the scan found, the service it answers as, and the size of its reply.
csv.sockets: Every socket the table showed when you saved it: who holds it, the two ends, its state, and when it opened, was first seen and closed.
cta.closing: Ready to break your own network on purpose?
cta.note: Free and open source under the GPLv3. Windows 10 and 11, 64-bit, and Linux as an experiment. No account, no telemetry.
exit.assertion: An assertion about the run did not hold.
exit.config: A setting or a value was invalid.
exit.io: A file could not be read or written.
exit.permission: No administrator rights, so the driver cannot load.
flag.cleanup_driver: Windows: unloads a capture driver left behind by an earlier run, which frees its locked file without a restart, then exits.
flag.config: Loads the settings from a JSON file, for example one saved from the window. A profile and the flags on the same line still override it.
flag.doctor: Checks this computer and exits: the rights a capture needs, the capture library and driver, leftovers in the temporary folder and a clock that jumped.
flag.dry_run: Checks the settings, a settings file and a scenario, then exits without loading the driver or touching any traffic. A cheap check for a pipeline.
flag.fail_on_no_traffic: The same as --min-packets 1: ends with exit code 6 when nothing was captured at all.
flag.format: The format of standard output: text for people, or json for a pipeline, one JSON object per line.
flag.gui: Opens the window. Only on its own: the window has its own controls, so it takes no settings from the command line.
flag.help: Prints every option with a short note, a few examples and the exit codes, then exits.
flag.install_desktop: Linux package only: adds the program to your desktop's applications menu, then exits. Run it as yourself, without sudo.
flag.interval: How often a report line is printed, in seconds: more than 0, at most 86400.
flag.license: Prints the licence and the notices of the third-party parts the program contains, then exits.
flag.log_conns: At the end, prints the connections the run saw.
flag.log_file: Also appends the log to this file.
flag.log_level: Sets the log level by name, and wins over -v and -q.
flag.loop: Plays the scenario again from the start each time it ends, until the run stops.
flag.min_packets: Ends with exit code 6 when fewer than this many packets were captured, which catches a traffic filter that matched nothing.
flag.preset: Loads a ready profile, by its id (presets.3g) or by its name in any language of the window ("3G network"). The profiles and their numbers are on the reference page.
flag.print_config: Prints the settings the run would use, after the defaults, the file, the profile and the flags, as JSON, and exits.
flag.quiet: Logs errors only, with no periodic reports.
flag.remove_desktop: Linux package only: removes that menu entry again, then exits.
flag.repro_out: At the end, writes a JSON report with the settings, the seed and the command that repeats the run.
flag.save_config: Writes the settings this command line adds up to into a JSON file and exits without starting anything. The window and --config can load the file.
flag.scenario: Plays a scenario file, a timeline that changes the settings at the seconds it names. A ready one can be named as scenarios/cafe-wifi.json from any folder.
flag.simulate: Runs on made-up traffic instead of a real capture: no driver, no administrator or root rights, and nothing on the network changes. For trying settings out and for tests.
flag.stop_on_stdin_close: Ends the run when standard input closes, as a normal end with its summary. A program that started this one stops it by closing the pipe, and if that program dies, the run ends at once instead of at --duration.
flag.verbose: Logs what the tool is doing: the settings it uses, the ports it found for a program, scenario steps, the driver opening and closing.
flag.version: Prints the program's version and exits.

llms.note: Aimed at testers, developers and QA who need to reproduce a bad connection on purpose. Impairment can be pointed at one process, PID, address or port, so the rest of the machine keeps working. Runs are repeatable with a seed, and the command line reports through exit codes and NDJSON, so a pipeline can use it. On Linux it runs as an experiment, from a package or from source. Not available for macOS.
llms.summary: Bean Network Tester is a free, open source (GNU GPL v3) Windows tool that deliberately degrades the network for one application: added latency and jitter, packet loss, corruption and duplication, download and upload speed limits, connection resets, link outages, port and address blocking, and LAN-only mode. It has a window and a command line in the same executable. Requires Windows 10 or 11, 64-bit, and administrator rights, because traffic is captured by the WinDivert driver. An experimental Linux package needs root rights and Linux 5.10 or newer. It sends nothing on its own - only the pings a user starts, to the address the user types.

ref.settings_window: These are in the {{app.windows.settings}} window, not on the {{app.app.tabs.control}} tab.
ref.switch: On or off (true or false in a file)
ref.when.live: Can change during a session, with {{app.buttons.apply}} or a scenario step
ref.when.view: Changes only what the window's tables show, at once
scenario.action.reset_tcp: Tears down the TCP connections in scope at that moment and holds them down for the step's duration, the way a dropped mobile connection does. It is the only action.
scenario.file.blocked-endpoint: One backend, 203.0.113.0/24, is blocked at 20 seconds while everything else keeps working, then unblocked. For timeouts, retries and fallbacks.
scenario.file.cafe-wifi: A cafe filling up: a decent link sinks to about 240 ms of ping, 6% loss and 2 Mbit/s, cutting out every 12 seconds at the worst, then recovers.
scenario.file.congested-vpn: A VPN whose upload collapses while the download stays fine, with latency spikes, an MTU of 1400 and occasional resets.
scenario.file.failing-dns: Only DNS on port 53 degrades, goes completely dead for 13 seconds and comes back, while everything else keeps working.
scenario.file.mobile-lte-to-3g: A phone walking out of LTE coverage: down to 3G, a full outage with a TCP reset at 60 seconds, a partial recovery, and back to LTE.
scenario.file.overloaded-game-server: A server sagging under load: ping, jitter, loss and duplication climb together, with spikes of up to 800 ms.
scenario.file.same-loss-in-runs: The same 5% loss the whole time, arriving four ways: evenly, then in runs of 5, 15 and 40 packets. For testing how an app reconnects.
scenario.file.upload-drop-midway: An upload that starts healthy, degrades, is cut to zero midway with a TCP reset, then partly recovers. For resumable uploads and progress bars.
scenario.key.action: Something to do once, at that second, instead of a setting that stays. A step needs settings, an action or both.
scenario.key.at: Required in every step: the second, counted from the start of the session, at which the step applies. Steps are sorted by it, so their order in the file does not matter.
scenario.key.duration: How long the action lasts, in seconds: more than 0, at most {max_action}, and 3 when left out. Only together with an action.
scenario.key.loop: Optional, false when left out. With true, the timeline starts again after the last step's time. The last step then lasts only a moment, so to hold a final phase, add a later step.
scenario.key.settings: The settings to change, under the same names as in a saved settings file. Only what a step names changes; everything else keeps the value an earlier step gave it.
scenario.key.steps: Required: the list of steps. A file may also be the bare list, [ ... ], which then does not repeat. At most {max_steps} steps.
setting.asym: Gives uploads their own numbers, because real home and mobile links are rarely the same in both directions. While it is on, the latency, jitter, spike, loss, corruption and duplication settings apply to downloads only, and the upload settings below apply to uploads. In the window they start as copies, so nothing changes until you edit them.
setting.block_ip: Drops all traffic to these remote addresses, in the same syntax as the address filter. A packet is blocked when it matches the address or the port. Other traffic is not affected.
setting.block_port: Drops all traffic to these remote ports. A packet is blocked when it matches the address or the port, so 443 alone blocks every HTTPS connection.
setting.block_reject: Refuses a blocked connection instead of leaving it unanswered, so the program reports "connection refused" within about two seconds, as with a port that is really closed, rather than waiting out its own timeout. TCP only, and only for connections this computer starts.
setting.buffer: How much delay a speed-limited link may queue up before it starts dropping packets. A large buffer gives bufferbloat: the speed is right, but every reply waits behind the queue. 0 means the queue has no limit. It matters only while a speed limit or a schedule is set.
setting.call_checks: Impairs only STUN messages: the connectivity and consent checks of calls that use ICE, such as WebRTC, keepalives and questions to a STUN server, through a relay too. Without answers to its consent checks, a call has to stop sending after 30 seconds. While any of the three call switches is on, everything else, blocking included, is left alone.
setting.call_media: Impairs only what a call carries: the DTLS handshake, audio and video (RTP) and data channels, directly or through a relay. A flow counts once it has carried STUN, so other UDP traffic, such as QUIC or a VPN, is left alone.
setting.call_turn_control: Impairs only the TURN messages that get and keep a relay: Allocate, Refresh, CreatePermission and ChannelBind. What the relay carries is left alone. Without them a call gets no relay at the start, and a relay it already has stops passing data within about 5 minutes.
setting.corrupt: The share of packets that arrive with one bit of their data flipped. Tests how a program copes with damaged data.
setting.corrupt_up: The share of sent packets that arrive with damaged data. Used only while separate upload values are on.
setting.down: The most a download may carry, in kilobytes per second. 0 means no limit. Ping uses tiny packets, so a speed limit hardly changes it; test a speed limit with a download.
setting.dst_ip: Limits the impairment to traffic to and from these remote addresses, IPv4 and IPv6: single addresses, lists, ranges, CIDR blocks, wildcards or re: patterns, with ! to leave one out. Empty means any address. With a port set too, traffic has to match both. Everything else passes unchanged.
setting.dst_port: Limits the impairment to these remote ports: numbers, lists, ranges or comparisons such as >1024, with ! to leave one out. Empty means any port. With an address set too, traffic has to match both.
setting.dup: The share of packets that arrive twice, a real symptom of a poor network.
setting.dup_up: The share of sent packets that arrive twice. Used only while separate upload values are on.
setting.duration: Stops the session by itself after this many seconds. 0 means it runs until you stop it. On the command line, a scenario that does not repeat also ends the run when its timeline does.
setting.filter: Which traffic the tool captures at all. What it leaves out passes untouched and is not counted. This list chooses directions, protocols and loopback; to aim at one address or port, use {{app.frames.destination}}.
setting.flap_down: How much of each period the link is down. 40 with a period of 10 seconds means 4 seconds down and 6 up, over and over.
setting.flap_hold: Packets that arrive during an outage wait and are delivered in order when it ends, instead of being dropped. This is what a Wi-Fi handover or a radio waking from sleep looks like to a program. Latency is added after the wait, and a speed limit spreads the burst out. At most 10,000 packets wait in one outage; the rest are dropped.
setting.flap_period: Repeated full outages: every this many seconds, the link goes down for part of the time, like a weak Wi-Fi that keeps dropping. 0 turns it off.
setting.internet_only: The opposite of the switch before it: cuts the local network (10.x, 192.168.x, 172.16-31.x, link-local, CGNAT) and keeps the internet. Loopback keeps working. If this computer asks the router for DNS, names stop resolving too, because those questions are local traffic.
setting.ipv4_only: Impairs IPv4 traffic only. IPv6 keeps flowing: it is not blocked, just left alone. It applies with the address list empty too.
setting.ipv6_only: Impairs IPv6 traffic only. IPv4 keeps flowing. With both switches on, nothing is left to impair, and the log says so.
setting.jitter: A random change to the delay, drawn for each packet, so ping wobbles instead of staying steady, and packets can arrive slightly out of order. Ping wobbles by more than this number, usually about 1.4 times, because the request and the reply each get their own draw.
setting.jitter_up: The random change to the upload delay. Used only while separate upload values are on.
setting.lan_mode: Cuts the internet and keeps the local network: traffic to and from public addresses is dropped, while 10.x, 192.168.x, 172.16-31.x and loopback keep working. On its own, with nothing else set, it already cuts this computer's internet.
setting.latency: Delay added to every packet. With traffic in both directions selected, the request and the reply are both delayed, so ping rises by about twice this number.
setting.latency_up: Delay added to packets this computer sends. Used only while separate upload values are on.
setting.loss: The share of packets that disappear without a trace. Even 5 percent feels like a connection that keeps dropping.
setting.loss_burst: Makes the loss arrive in runs: the number is how many packets are lost in a row on average, while the share of lost packets stays the same. A run of losses hurts a connection far more than the same loss spread out. 0 spreads it evenly.
setting.loss_up: The share of sent packets that disappear. Used only while separate upload values are on.
setting.max_size: Drops packets larger than this many bytes: the MTU black hole common with tunnels and VPNs, where small packets pass and large ones vanish. 0 turns it off.
setting.narrow_filter: Makes the tool look only at the addresses and ports set under {{app.frames.destination}} and ignore everything else on the computer, so it keeps up with more packets. The statistics and the connections then show only that traffic. It works with plain addresses, ports and ranges; a wildcard, an re: pattern or a program alone leaves it with no effect.
setting.nat_timeout: Forgets a connection that stays silent for longer than this many seconds, the way a home router's NAT does: the next packet coming in is dropped. Tests keepalives. 0 turns it off.
setting.payload_tcp: Impairs only TCP packets that carry this many bytes of data: !0 leaves bare acknowledgements alone. With only this one filled in, UDP is left alone; with both filled in, each packet is checked against the one for its own protocol.
setting.payload_udp: Impairs only UDP packets that carry this many bytes of data, headers not counted, in the same syntax as the other filters: 64-1472 leaves small keepalives alone. With only this one filled in, TCP is left alone. Packets whose size cannot be read, such as ICMP or fragments, always pass.
setting.rate_schedule: A speed that changes over time, played in a loop: steps of seconds:download:upload in kilobytes per second, separated by commas. 2:100:0, 2:500:0 means 2 seconds at 100 KB/s, then 2 seconds at 500. While it is set, it replaces the download and upload limits.
setting.row_limit: The most rows a table in the window shows. The tables draw only what is on screen, so a high limit costs nothing to draw; it only limits the work of filtering and sorting. 0 shows everything.
setting.rst_cooldown: How long a connection stays blocked after a reset.
setting.rst_prob: The chance that a TCP packet resets its connection with an injected RST. TCP only; UDP has no reset.
setting.seed: Makes the random parts of a run, such as which packets are lost, repeat exactly the next time with the same settings, which turns an occasional bug into one you can reproduce. Empty or -1 picks a new seed each time.
setting.spike_ms: The extra delay a packet gets when a spike hits it, on top of the latency. To reorder packets, make it larger than the gap between them.
setting.spike_ms_up: The extra delay a sent packet gets when a spike hits it, on top of the latency. Used only while separate upload values are on.
setting.spike_prob: How often a single packet gets a much longer delay, in percent of packets. A delayed packet arrives after ones sent later, so this also changes the order of packets.
setting.spike_prob_up: How often a sent packet gets a much longer delay. Used only while separate upload values are on.
setting.syn_drop: The share of TCP SYN packets, the ones that open a connection, that are dropped. A connection then opens late or not at all, which tests retry logic.
setting.target: Limits every setting to the programs you name: process names, PIDs, ranges, wildcards or re: patterns, separated by commas, with ! in front of one to leave it out. Empty means all traffic. A program named by its name is found again after it restarts; one named by its PID is not.
setting.up: The most an upload may carry, in kilobytes per second. 0 means no limit.
